## What do we mean by "API"?

Not a web API. When I say API in this talk, I mean the literal
**function signature** — the contract for how you interact with a piece
of code.

```r
sum(x, na.rm = TRUE) # The `sum` API

df %>% select(...) # `DataFrame` or `select` API
```

```python
data.filter(pl.col('truthy')) # `DataFrame` or `filter` API

[x + 1 for x in vec] # List comprehension API
```

Some APIs are more theoretical in nature:

```default
Imperative vs. Procedural

RDBMS vs. Graph

UV Projects vs. Virtual Environments
```

::: {.notes}
Clarify before going further: this talk is not about REST/web APIs.
An API here just means the shape of the function — the arguments you
pass in, the value you get back — the contract you have to learn to
use something.
:::

No one asks the principal character - the programmer doing the migration.

## I'm trying to install python… {.bullets-lg}

::: {.incremental}
- What is pip, conda, pyenv?
- What's an interpreter?
- What's a path?
- VSCode has python in it right?
:::

::: {.notes}
Cold open, first person, present tense — pre-uv world: pip, conda, pyenv,
interpreters, paths.

Everyone in the room who's installed Python has lived some version of
this. Let the laugh land, then turn it: the first impression isn't a
footnote — it sets the tone for everything that follows.

Keep this to one beat — there are whole talks just on Python packaging.
:::

## Takeaway: {.center}

::: {.fragment .big-word}
APIs matter.
:::

## Thesis: {.center}

::: {.fragment .big-word}
*Language migrations should emphasize the easiest option for the principal agent, the programmer.*
:::

::: {.notes}
The hot take: APIs matter more than speed, cost, or support.

State it plainly and let the rest of the talk earn it — this is the one
decision that determines how much friction the team absorbs.
:::

# The easy migration

::: {.notes}
I want to outline what goes into an easy migration
:::

## *Chapter One: Getting started fast* {.bullets-lg}

::: {.incremental}
- [Early]{.accent} wins

- The [thin-slice]{.accent} effect
:::

::: {.notes}
The question we're answering here is - Can I be productive immediately?

Getting started in a new coding workflow is important. Not only for timelines but to generate interest in the new language.

[click] early wins

Pick the API that lets people write real code on day one, before they've mastered environments, classes, or types.

Getting some early code typed up and working is impactful to superiors and makes you feel good.

[click] First impressions

First impressions are not necessarily accurate, but they have more predictive power and persistence than we would like to believe.

Thin-slicing literature unequivically indicates we are judgemental animals, predicting trends constantly. Even a slice of an interaction with something new can deeply inform our opinions of it in the long term.

This isn't right, but it's reality, and it's something that has to be managed.
:::

::: {.notes}
Pillar One: Getting Started Fast
Make this about activation energy and the first 30 minutes/day.
Your selector/aggregation example is good here, but I'd use the simplest
possible version. You don't want to explain the code; you want the
audience to recognize it instantly.

Chapter One: Getting Started Fast
Early wins matter.
First impressions matter.
Pick the API that lets people write real, useful code on day one.
Don't make the first lesson environments, classes, types, or package
management.
Friction at the start compounds.

Then your cocktail analogy works here. The core idea is:
The first experience determines whether people keep going.
The code demo should therefore show "I just learned this and
immediately accomplished something."

The audience takeaway is simply:
"Holy shit, I can already do real work."
Don't get into the philosophy yet.
:::

## Conclusion: {.center}

::: {.fragment .big-word}
*Framework and Language API is a first class consideration.*
:::

::: {.notes}
Not all APIs are created equal — some are just thin wrappers exposing
every private method.

User-friendly frameworks pay dividends early, while people are still
coming up to speed on everything else.

The goal is comfort, not full control of a complex system.
:::

## *Pillar Two: Keep the same shape of thought* {.bullets-lg}

::: {.incremental}
- Easy [syntax]{.accent} is a virtue
- Import your [philosophy]{.accent}
:::

::: {.notes}
Same shape of thought: don't make people relearn how to think about data.

[click] Easy syntax — other options leaned on verbose, heavily-typed
languages that added friction before anyone got to the actual work.

[click] Import your philosophy — we chose Polars because its
expression-based API preserved the dplyr way of thinking about data,
not just its syntax.
:::

## Code snippet on similarities in syntax/philosophy

`sum(revenue[status == "paid"])` becomes:

```python
pl.col("revenue")
  .filter(pl.col("status") == "paid")
  .sum()
```

::: {.fragment}
**Same thought. Different language.**
:::

::: {.notes}
This is about transfer, not onboarding: once you know the syntax, does
the system let you keep thinking about data the way you already do?

The dplyr mental model transfers directly — select, transform, filter,
aggregate — with no detour through OOP, strong typing, or imperative
loops.

Same thought. Different language. That's the actual migration story.
:::

## Pillar two conclusion: {.center}

::: {.fragment .big-word}
Some days, you don't need to learn anything new.
:::

::: {.notes}
Migrating is already information overload — it doesn't all have to land
on day one. You don't take Calc 4 before Calc 1.

Once people are comfortable, they'll move on to the fancier stuff on
their own, and make better-informed decisions about it.
:::

## Pillar Three: Morale {.bullets-lg}

::: {.incremental}
- Maintain early consistency
- Reduce fear
:::

::: {.notes}
A migration is already disruptive — morale is the resource you're
protecting.

[click] Maintain early consistency — shared idioms make code easier to
read, review, and debug, so the team isn't each having a different
experience of the same migration.

[click] Reduce fear — keep as much of the team's existing mental model
as possible. Early wins build confidence, and confidence keeps people
engaged.
:::
